title: School Students Confidence When Answering Diagnostic Questions Online https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10649-021-10084-7
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), October 21, 2025 — original paper:
summary: This page covers Foster, Woodhead, Barton, and Clark-Wilson's analysis of a large Eedi dataset of diagnostic multiple-choice maths questions answered by UK students aged six to sixteen, focusing on how self-reported confidence relates to performance (facility) and to demographic factors. Confidence correlates positively with facility overall, but boys report higher confidence than girls at the same attainment level, and older or socioeconomically disadvantaged students report lower confidence even after controlling for how well they actually perform. The paper also provides the first evidence of the hypercorrection effect, where high-confidence errors are more likely to be corrected later, in an authentic school-mathematics setting rather than only in laboratory conditions. Barton's summary draws out the practical implication that confidence ratings alongside diagnostic questions are not just a curiosity but a usable formative-assessment tool, one that can also surface demographic confidence gaps worth addressing directly. It cautions that the data comes from an online platform, so findings may not transfer perfectly to face-to-face classroom settings.
points: This study provides the first evidence for the hypercorrection effect in an authentic school-mathematics context, not just in laboratory settings; high-confidence errors are more likely to be corrected later.
Boys report higher confidence than girls at the same level of attainment, while older and disadvantaged students report lower confidence even accounting for performance.
Pairing confidence ratings with diagnostic multiple-choice questions is an innovative, low-cost formative-assessment tool teachers can use to prompt reflection and improve metacognition over time.
Because errors made with high confidence are more likely to be corrected, trying to prevent students from making mistakes in low-stakes assessment may actually be counterproductive.
quotes: The academic article presents an analysis of a substantial, pre-existing dataset derived from the Eedi online platform, which features diagnostic multiple-choice mathematics questions for UK school students aged six to sixteen.

Key findings include a positive correlation between confidence and facility, with boys exhibiting higher confidence than girls and older students or socioeconomically disadvantaged students showing lower confidence, even when accounting for facility.

The study provides the first evidence of the hypercorrection effect—where highly confident errors are more likely to be corrected later—in an authentic school-mathematics context, with important implications for classroom learning practices.
Teachers should incorporate confidence assessment alongside diagnostic multiple-choice questions. This feature can serve as an innovative formative assessment tool.
Finally, we found the first evidence for the hypercorrection effect in an authentic mathematics learning context.
